prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my configuration is unchanged: a single-part B046 prize to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific arc is complete and independently confirmed for decades: proglucagon processing and GLP-1 biology (Drucker), secretion and insulinotropic action in humans (Holst), and the identification of the active truncated peptide (Mojsov), followed by randomized outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. Maturity is not in question. The citation names the hormone and its active form and the therapies only as a consequence, so it honours a discovery that changed the field and then medicine without endorsing any product. Round 1 showed that no member prefers a different or two-part configuration, but I treat that as a coincidence of judgments and not as evidence. What I tested is whether the attribution and scope objections would break the case, and they do not.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still credit, not science. Mojsov's priority on GLP-1(7-36) is contested, Habener is outside the credited names, and Knudsen's role in the long-acting analogues is excluded by the three-person cap. If the committee decides the achievement is the drug, this trio is incomplete and the citation would need rewriting around the therapies. A second objection, raised by Wahren-Herlenius, is that a one-part prize leaves CAR-T unrewarded this year. I do not think that is a reason to dilute B046, since pairing would force one of the three names out. Nothing in the supplied text lets me settle the Mojsov-Habener question, so a public verdict on it remains a risk I accept knowingly.

responses.point: The chair asked whether the citation should honour physiology or drug development and whether Knudsen should replace Mojsov, and proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen in round 1.
responses.response: I have re-weighed this and I keep Mojsov. Four colleagues independently reached the same view for the same reason: Knudsen's half-life engineering depends on knowing what the active peptide is and what it does, and replacing a discovery credit with a development credit changes the prize from discovery to drug design. I accept your point that long-acting analogues are a genuine scientific achievement and not routine engineering, and I note that Linnarsson has already moved Knudsen out of his proposal. If the committee decides the citation should name the medicines, I would put Knudsen forward, but she would then have to displace someone, and I would not choose Drucker or Holst. Mojsov's priority is contested, but a contested claim is not a refuted one, and excluding her by default would settle the matter without evidence.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks cGAS-STING fourth, notes human genetic confirmation but no approved therapy, rejects a third name because Ishikawa's priority is unresolved, and says CAR-T is a clear second that she would pair with B046 only for a two-part prize.
responses.response: You moved me on cGAS-STING. In round 1 I ranked it second and listed it as an alternative. Your point that human genetic disease (STING-associated vasculopathy, Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome) shows the pathway matters, while the medical payoff is still prospective, is the right framing, and El Manira, Linnarsson, Sandberg and Svenningsson made the same maturity argument. I now drop B029 from my alternatives for this year. On pairing, I do not support adding CAR-T to B046. The three-name cap would force a B046 name out, and no one has proposed which, so a two-part configuration would trade a coherent trio for a weaker pair of parts. I would accept your long-term safety point as a reason for care in wording, not for waiting.

responses.point: Linnarsson considers CAR-T the next most robust candidate if priority on GLP-1 cannot be settled, with June, Sadelain and Rosenberg, and would reopen Rosenberg if a prize were built around CAR-T.
responses.response: I still regard CAR-T as the strongest challenger, with approved products and durable remissions, and I would not object to it as a later prize. My reservation remains attribution. Eshhar's early chimeric-receptor concept is outside the credited names, and Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is broader than the engineered receptor, which Sandberg also argued. June and Sadelain alone would be cleaner, but then the origin of the concept is still unaddressed. That is a harder credit problem than B046, where the physiology trio is internally coherent even though Mojsov's priority is disputed. So I have not added B028 to my alternatives. I would revisit that if the committee can show a fair allocation that includes Eshhar's role.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks SMN2 antisense (B007) second as a clean mechanism-to-therapy story and says that if a majority prefers a development-inclusive prize, Drucker, Holst and Knudsen is coherent.
responses.response: I agree that B007 has a clean two-name credit and a striking clinical effect, and I accept your openness to a development-inclusive B046. I remain where I was on B007: the treated population is small, the credit is split between splicing mechanism and oligonucleotide chemistry, and the SMN1 gene discovery (Melki and Lefebvre, as Wahren-Herlenius noted) lies outside the credited pair, so it would be a harder citation to write. On your conditional, I do not want to rule out Drucker, Holst and Knudsen on the science, but the grounds for preferring it would have to be that drug development is the achievement. Nobody has argued that to my satisfaction, and your own round-1 reasoning favoured Mojsov.

responses.point: El Manira asks to see the evidence on who first characterised the active GLP-1 form before choosing, would revisit Mojsov if the record is too uncertain, and ranks the unfolded protein response third with Walter and Mori.
responses.response: This is the open question and I cannot answer it from the supplied text, so I am not claiming to have resolved it. What I can say is that no member has shown that Habener's claim is stronger than Mojsov's, and the burden should be on the argument for exclusion. I agree with your assessment of B011: Walter and Mori are a compact, mature credit. I have moved it into my alternatives in place of B029, because an exact credit and a stable framework weigh more with me than a still-prospective therapeutic case. I keep B038 as the other alternative. I share your caution that it is a tool and that six names compete for three places.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Habener has the stronger documented claim on the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, which I cannot settle from the supplied text.
Whether the committee wants the citation centred on physiology or on drug development, which determines whether Knudsen should enter the configuration at all and at whose expense.
Whether long-term safety and central-mechanism questions for GLP-1 agonists should affect wording; I think not, but I hold this with moderate confidence.
Whether B011 and B038 belong in the same tier as alternatives; both are mature in a different sense and neither is a disease-level therapy.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on any shortlisted ballot. Documented collaborations with Ronald Evans and Johan Ericson, and about twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson and one with Abdel El Manira (2009), involve no credited candidate. My nuclear-receptor and dopamine-neuron research does not overlap with any shortlisted discovery. No change since round 1.
